Energy-driven monetary squeeze

Thread · Energy-driven monetary squeeze

Washington pairs Iran outreach with strike preparations while oil and inflation keep central banks on hold

Current direction. Diplomatic outreach and strike preparation are running in parallel in Washington. Oil prices ease on each sign of talks but stay above $110 a barrel, and both the Fed and the ECB hold rates rather than ease.

Read the full thread analysis

Where it comes from. The US-Israeli war with Iran is in its ninth month, and Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed to traffic it does not authorise. Oil has carried a Middle East risk premium since the fighting began, and euro-area inflation reached a three-year high of 3.8% in September.

What is driving it underneath. Washington is pursuing talks and preparing renewed strikes at the same time, with the Nov. 3 midterms as the reference date. Each turn between the two moves the oil price, and oil feeds directly into the inflation figures that central banks are weighing.

Who is driving it, and toward what.

  • Trump administration
    Aim: The administration seeks an end to the war on terms that reopen shipping lanes, according to US officials quoted on the G20 agenda.
    Evidence: Vice President JD Vance reached out to Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei to restart negotiations, the Wall Street Journal reported. The Associated Press reported that US officials told Middle East governments to be ready for renewed strikes after the midterms.
    Says vs does: Washington describes free passage for shipping as its top G20 priority, while it also prepares regional partners for renewed military action. [1] [2]
  • Iranian government
    Aim: Tehran demands that the United States meet its conditions first, including lifting the US naval blockade and releasing frozen assets, according to ISW's reading of Rezaei's views.
    Evidence: A senior Iranian official rejected the US and Qatari proposals as unacceptable, CNBC reported. [1] [8]
  • European Central Bank
    Aim: The ECB says its task is to bring inflation back to its 2% goal.
    Evidence: The Governing Council unanimously held the deposit rate at 2.5% on Oct. 29, even as euro-area inflation stood at 3.8%. [7] [6]

What's at stake.

  • Gulf states: Saudi Arabia, a G20 member, hosts oil assets and US forces within range of Iranian and Houthi retaliation.
  • Euro-area governments: High energy prices push inflation up and keep the cost of servicing their debt high.
  • Iran: Tehran seeks the release of frozen assets and the lifting of the US naval blockade.

The tensions.

  • Coercion vs diplomacy: Washington tells partners to prepare for strikes while its vice president reaches out to Tehran.
  • Inflation vs growth: The ECB holds rates at 2.5% because higher rates could deter investment while inflation runs at 3.8%.

What we don't know. N o s o u r c e s t a t e s w h a t t e r m s t h e Q a t a r i p r o p o s a l c o n t a i n s . T h e E C B h a s n o t s a i d w h o i t s c a n d i d a t e s t o s u c c e e d C h r i s t i n e L a g a r d e a r e .

Competing readings. Some read the outreach to Rezaei as a real attempt to end the war before the midterms. Others, including ISW, read Iran's stated conditions as too far from US terms for the letter to restart talks, and Control Risks told Bloomberg that military action near the midterms is not its base case.

How today's events connect.

  • Brent fell 44 cents to $114.88 on Oct. 29 because traders weighed the renewed US outreach to Iran, and that affects fuel import bills in every oil-importing economy.
  • The ECB held its rate because energy-driven inflation sits well above target while growth is weak, and that affects borrowers across the euro area, including a French state facing rising borrowing costs.
  • US PCE inflation rose to 3.6% in September because fuel stayed expensive, and that affects how long the Federal Reserve keeps its 3.75% to 4% range.

Counter-forces.

  • Qatari mediators
    Why it resists: Qatar put forward a fresh proposal to end the conflict, which keeps a negotiating track open.
  • Senior Iranian officials
    Why it resists: A senior Iranian official rejected the proposals, which keeps the risk premium in oil prices.

What's unresolved. Sources do not say whether Iran has formally answered the Vance outreach. The timing and scale of any US military action after Nov. 3 are not public. [1] [2] [7] [6] [9] [8]

Central banks, inflation and debt ■ steady

What happened. The ECB's Governing Council unanimously left its deposit rate at 2.5% on Oct. 29, with euro-area inflation at 3.8% in September, a three-year high. Christine Lagarde said she will step down as ECB president on Feb. 7, 2027, almost nine months early. US PCE inflation rose 0.5% in September to an annual 3.6%, and third-quarter GDP grew at an annualised 3.4%. [7] [6] [9] Established

Context. Energy prices rose sharply after the war with Iran began, pushing inflation above the 2% targets of both the ECB and the Federal Reserve. Both banks raised rates again this year and now hold them at restrictive levels.

Who is Christine Lagarde ECB president since November 2019, a former French finance minister and head of the IMF from 2011 to 2019.

Who is António Costa President of the European Council, who said the search for Lagarde's successor starts immediately.

What changed. The rate hold matches the arc's restrictive plateau. Lagarde's early exit is the first leadership break in the arc's record, and the 3.6% PCE reading is above the 1.6% to 2.4% baseline range.

Why now. Higher rates would curb energy-driven inflation but also weigh on investment and growth, so the ECB holds. DW reports speculation that Lagarde is leaving early so EU leaders can pick her successor before France's spring presidential election.

Who gains, who loses. EU governments gain control of the succession timetable before the French vote. Euro-area borrowers face rates that stay at 2.5%, and US borrowers face a Fed range of 3.75% to 4% that strong growth gives little reason to cut.

Counterview. Lagarde said she is leaving to gain freedom to engage on matters beyond monetary policy, and no reason tied to the French election has been confirmed.

Link. Elections and political shifts worldwide: Lagarde's departure date places the choice of her successor before France's presidential election in the spring.

Thread · Great-power realignment

Russia keeps striking Ukrainian cities as its foreign minister joins the G20 in Atlanta

Current direction. Russia's long-range strikes on Ukrainian cities continue at the same time as US-led diplomacy. Kyiv has resumed refinery strikes despite Washington's earlier pressure to stop them.

Read the full thread analysis

Where it comes from. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Western sanctions on Russian officials followed. The United States now hosts the Group of 20, whose members remain divided over the war.

What is driving it underneath. Washington is pushing a peace process and asked Kyiv to pause refinery strikes, while Moscow keeps up drone and missile attacks. The G20 gives Russia a table in the United States at which to contest Western sanctions.

Who is driving it, and toward what.

  • Russian government
    Aim: Moscow seeks relief from Western sanctions, and Lavrov plans to criticise them at the Atlanta meeting, according to the Kyiv Post.
    Evidence: A Russian jet-powered drone hit a crowded platform at Dnipro's main railway station on Oct. 29, killing at least 14 people.
    Says vs does: Moscow denies deliberately targeting civilians, while its drones keep hitting Ukraine's railway network, including a platform with passenger trains standing at it. [3] [4]
  • Ukrainian government
    Aim: Kyiv seeks more US, European and G7 sanctions on Russia and keeps hitting Russian oil revenue.
    Evidence: Ukraine hit a Russian oil refinery, ending a two-week pause in refinery attacks that followed US pressure, the Wall Street Journal reported. [4] [5] [22]
  • Marco Rubio
    Aim: The US secretary of state chairs the G20 foreign ministers and has named free passage for shipping as Washington's top priority for the meeting.
    Evidence: Washington admitted Lavrov to the Oct. 30-31 meeting despite objections from Republican Don Bacon and Democrat Jeanne Shaheen. [2] [3]

What's at stake.

  • Ukraine: Kyiv risks losing US support if it defies Washington, and risks losing leverage if it gives up refinery strikes.
  • Russia: Moscow gains standing from a seat at a US-hosted meeting while under sanctions.
  • United States: Washington's credibility as a G20 chair and peace broker depends on producing results from both tracks.

The tensions.

  • Peace process vs pressure on Moscow: Washington hosts Russia's foreign minister while Ukraine and European capitals call for tighter sanctions.
  • Alliance management vs Ukrainian autonomy: Kyiv paused refinery strikes under US pressure, then resumed them two weeks later.

What we don't know. T h e R u s s i a n m i l i t a r y h a s n o t c o m m e n t e d o n t h e D n i p r o s t r i k e . T h e W S J r e p o r t d o e s n o t n a m e t h e r e f i n e r y U k r a i n e h i t i n t h i s s u m m a r y .

Competing readings. Bacon and Shaheen argue that welcoming Lavrov rewards Moscow while it attacks civilians. The Trump administration's case is that a peace process needs Russia at the table, and the G20 host has to admit member delegations.

How today's events connect.

  • Ukraine paused refinery strikes because of complaints from President Trump, and its renewed strike affects how far Washington can steer Kyiv's targeting.
  • US lawmakers objected to Lavrov's visit because of the Dnipro deaths, and that affects the politics of the Atlanta meeting for its American host.

Counter-forces.

  • Don Bacon and Jeanne Shaheen
    Why it resists: The two senators from opposite parties publicly opposed Lavrov's welcome in Washington.
  • European leaders
    Why it resists: They reacted with outrage to the Dnipro attack, which adds pressure for more sanctions rather than less.

What's unresolved. Sources do not say whether Washington objected to Ukraine's renewed refinery strike. No date is public for the new peace talks that Washington is preparing. [4] [3] [2] [5] [22]

Thread · Great-power realignment · Technology decoupling

China's military build-up meets denser US-Japan-Philippine cooperation and a new chip-security case

Current direction. Allied defence integration is deepening, with production moving into Japan and US equipment staged closer to China. Chinese naval deployments are spreading across three neighbouring areas at once.

Read the full thread analysis

Where it comes from. China has expanded its navy and increased incursions into waters the Philippines claims over the past few years. Since 2021, US planning in the Pacific has been organised around the so-called Davidson window, a warning that China could be able to act against Taiwan by 2027.

What is driving it underneath. Beijing is building conventional military power without explaining its aims, according to Australia's defence minister. Washington and its allies are responding with forward deployments, co-production and tighter control of advanced chips.

Who is driving it, and toward what.

  • Chinese government
    Aim: Beijing claims Taiwan as its territory and presses its claims in the South China Sea.
    Evidence: Taiwan's National Security Council head Joseph Wu shared a map of 53 Chinese vessels, including 34 warships and the carrier Liaoning, operating from southern Japan to the Philippines. [32] [33]
  • US Army Pacific
    Aim: Gen. Ronald Clark said the command is setting the theatre to be ready by 2027.
    Evidence: Under Army Ready Forward, the command keeps equipment, materiel and rotating troops west of the International Date Line on the island chains closest to China. [34]
  • Japanese government
    Aim: Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi called the missile co-production deal a groundbreaking agreement for both countries.
    Evidence: Koizumi and Pete Hegseth agreed on Oct. 28 to build a final assembly and test facility for AMRAAM missiles in Japan. [35]

What's at stake.

  • Taiwan: Its security depends on deterrence by US and allied forces that are still positioning.
  • South Korea: Chosun Biz reports that Seoul's role in US regional planning is narrowing as Japan becomes the main production and logistics hub.
  • Nvidia: Its access to Washington depends on trust that its chips are not reaching China against US export rules.

The tensions.

  • Deterrence vs escalation: Allied forward deployments aim to deter, while Beijing presents them as pressure on China.
  • Commercial reach vs security controls: Nvidia says close contact with partners is part of a CEO's job, while US officials surveilled one of those partners as a suspected spy.

What we don't know. S o u r c e s d o n o t g i v e a c o s t o r p r o d u c t i o n v o l u m e f o r t h e A M R A A M f a c i l i t y i n J a p a n . T h e s c o p e o f A l i c e H u a n g ' s a c c e s s t o J e n s e n H u a n g i s r e p o r t e d o n l y t h r o u g h u n n a m e d s o u r c e s .

Competing readings. Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles describes China's build-up as the biggest conventional build-up since the Second World War. Beijing accused Manila of obstructing its attendance at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) defence meeting, and Chinese officials frame their activity as a response to US alliance moves.

How today's events connect.

  • US Army Pacific keeps equipment in the first island chain because commanders still plan around the 2027 window, and that puts Japan and the Philippines at the centre of US readiness.
  • White House officials are alarmed because a suspected Chinese asset had close ties to Jensen Huang, and that affects trust in the Nvidia channel the administration relies on.

Counter-forces.

  • Chinese government
    Why it resists: Beijing disputes the allied framing and contested its treatment at the ASEAN meeting in Cebu.
  • Nvidia
    Why it resists: The company says earlier diversion allegations were investigated and debunked.

What's unresolved. Sources do not say how long the Chinese deployment east of the Philippines will last. No US agency has publicly confirmed the intelligence finding about Alice Huang. [33] [32] [34] [35] [36]

STRUCTURAL FORCE

Electoral anger meets institutions

Thread · Electoral anger meets institutions

Contested handovers of power in Israel, Brazil and Venezuela, with US midterms four days away

Current direction. Losing or threatened camps contest results in Brazil and Venezuela, while electoral authorities and courts uphold them. In Israel, coalition bargaining has begun with no bloc able to govern alone.

Read the full thread analysis

Where it comes from. Israel's Oct. 27 vote was its first election since the Hamas attack of Oct. 7, 2023. Brazil held its presidential run-off on Oct. 25, and Venezuela has had an interim government since the United States seized Nicolás Maduro in January.

What is driving it underneath. Voters are punishing incumbents and governments seen as failing on security or living costs. Coalition rules, courts and election authorities then decide how far that anger changes who governs.

Who is driving it, and toward what.

  • Gadi Eisenkot
    Aim: The former military chief leads the opposition alliance that campaigned to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
    Evidence: Neither his alliance nor Netanyahu's bloc won a majority, and Arab-led parties won a historic 19 seats. [42]
  • Flávio Bolsonaro
    Aim: The far-right senator says he will lead Brazil's opposition from the United States.
    Evidence: He lost the run-off to Lula by 4.4 million votes, left Brazil without surrendering his passports and called himself leader of Brazil in a letter.
    Says vs does: He alleges fraud without evidence, while Brazil's electoral authority says the vote ran normally and both campaigns asked for the extended polling hours he now disputes. [43]
  • María Corina Machado
    Aim: The Venezuelan opposition leader seeks a presidential election in 2027, which she says the United States proposed.
    Evidence: She returned to Caracas from nearly a year in exile and called the transition irreversible. [44]

What's at stake.

  • Benjamin Netanyahu: He stays in office as caretaker only while no rival coalition forms.
  • Arab-led parties in Israel: Their 19 seats give them a possible role in forming a government for the first time on this scale.
  • Venezuelan voters: They wait for a date for the presidential vote that Machado and Rodríguez both say will happen.

The tensions.

  • Popular anger vs institutional checks: Bolsonaro disputes his defeat, while Brazil's electoral authority and a BBC Verify analysis find no basis for his claim.
  • Coalition arithmetic vs voter expectations: Israel's opposition can reach a majority only through partners its own voters may reject.

What we don't know. S o u r c e s d o n o t d e t a i l w h e t h e r U S a u t h o r i t i e s h a v e g r a n t e d B o l s o n a r o a f o r m a l i m m i g r a t i o n s t a t u s . T h e f i n a l s e a t t o t a l s f o r e a c h I s r a e l i p a r t y a r e n o t i n t o d a y ' s s o u r c e s .

Competing readings. Supporters of Israel's opposition read the result as a rejection of Netanyahu's government, since the opposition parties won about 55% of the vote. Netanyahu's camp can point out that he has not lost and that any alternative majority depends on Arab parties that most of the Jewish opposition rejects as partners.

How today's events connect.

  • Netanyahu stays on as caretaker because no bloc won a majority, and that affects how Israel's side of any US-Iran deal is negotiated.
  • Venezuela's transition runs on a US timetable because Washington seized Maduro and backed Rodríguez, and that gives the United States a hand in when Venezuelans vote.

Counter-forces.

  • Brazil's electoral authority
    Why it resists: Its head said the vote proceeded normally and in full accordance with the law.
  • Delcy Rodríguez
    Why it resists: Venezuela's interim president says her government should oversee the transition and has set no date for elections.

What's unresolved. Sources do not say which Israeli coalition is being negotiated first. No date has been set for Venezuela's presidential election. [42] [45] [43] [44] [46]

Elections and political shifts worldwide ■ steady

What happened. Final results released on Oct. 30 confirm that neither Netanyahu's bloc nor the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot can form a government alone. Arab-led parties won a historic 19 seats. Netanyahu stays on as caretaker while coalition talks begin. [42] [45] [47] Established

Benjamin NetanyahuPrime minister of Israel and leader of the right-wing blocPhoto credit [48]GEGadi EisenkotFormer Israeli military chiefNo licensed portrait found; initials shown.AArab-led partiesArab citizens of IsraelNo licensed portrait found; initials shown.
Read the full analysis

Context. Israel's Oct. 27 election was the first since the Hamas attack of Oct. 7, 2023, and Israel has since fought Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iran. Turnout reached almost 78%, seven points higher than in the previous election and the highest since 1999.

Who is Benjamin Netanyahu Prime minister of Israel and leader of the right-wing bloc, now serving as caretaker.

Who is Gadi Eisenkot Former Israeli military chief who leads the opposition alliance known as the Change bloc.

Who's who and what a win means

  • Benjamin NetanyahuHis right-wing blocPhoto credit [48] His right-wing bloc, which won about 45% of the vote according to Open magazine. Positions: He has led Israel's multi-front war against Hamas, Hezbollah, the Houthis and Iran. Sources today do not detail his positions on Russia, the EU, NATO or the economy. Grievances behind their support: Sources do not detail his voters' grievances beyond national security after the Oct. 7 attack. If they win: A coalition he leads would keep the government that has run the war with Iran, though sources do not detail which partners he would add to reach a majority.
  • GEGadi EisenkotThe Change bloc of four parties that campaigned as a united front to rNo licensed portrait found; initials shown. The Change bloc of four parties that campaigned as a united front to replace Netanyahu. Positions: The bloc's stated aim is a change of Israel's leadership. Sources today do not detail its positions on Russia, the EU, NATO or the economy. Grievances behind their support: His voters channelled anger at the prime minister over national security and governance, in an election widely described as a referendum on both. If they win: A government he leads would need either Netanyahu's party or Arab-led parties, and either choice would require compromises that sources say could anger his own voters.
  • AArab-led partiesArab citizens of IsraelNo licensed portrait found; initials shown. Arab citizens of Israel, who gave these parties about 15% of the vote and 19 seats. Positions: Sources do not detail their platforms on foreign policy or the economy. Grievances behind their support: Sources do not detail the specific grievances behind their vote. If they win: Their support for an opposition government would give Arab parties a decisive role in forming a coalition on a scale sources call historic.

What changed. Partial counts on Oct. 28 and Oct. 29 showed the same deadlock. The final count confirms the result rather than changing it.

Why now. The opposition must choose between a unity government with Netanyahu, whom it campaigned against, and a partnership with Arab parties that most of the Jewish opposition finds unacceptable. If no coalition forms, AP reports that new elections follow.

Who gains, who loses. Netanyahu keeps his office during the Iran war while talks run. Arab-led parties gain bargaining power, and India's former ambassador Mahesh Sachdev says New Delhi's ties with Israel hold whoever governs.

Counterview. Netanyahu's bloc is the largest single camp, and his supporters argue that an opposition majority built on Arab parties does not reflect a Jewish-majority mandate for change.

Link. Middle East and the Iran axis: A caretaker government in Israel coincides with renewed US outreach to Iran and US briefings on possible strikes.

Connects to. Middle East and the Iran axis, Elections and political shifts worldwide. Driver: Coalition arithmetic after a security-focused election

What happened. Democrats led Republicans 51.4% to 43.2% in the RealClearPolling average four days before the vote. A Marquette Law School poll in Wisconsin put Trump's approval at 37% and found only 16% of respondents better off than a year ago. Trump cancelled weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa in favour of telephone events. [46] [51] Reported

Context. The United States holds midterm elections on Nov. 3 for Congress and many state offices. Trump's approval ratings are declining, and economic concerns are alarming Republicans, according to Marquette's Charles Franklin.

Who is Charles Franklin Director of the Marquette Law School Poll in Wisconsin.

Who is Elon Musk Billionaire entrepreneur who is campaigning against Democrats before the midterms.

Who is Donald Trump Republican US president in his second term.

What changed. Earlier entries recorded the run-up to the vote. The 8.2-point national gap and the cancelled rallies are new data points within the arc's existing record of an unpopular war.

Why now. Living costs and the war weigh on the president's party, according to Marquette's Charles Franklin. Elon Musk is campaigning against Democrats by warning about DC and Puerto Rico statehood, legal status for undocumented migrants and expanding the Supreme Court.

Who gains, who loses. Democrats gain enthusiasm, Franklin says. Republicans in competitive races lose the president's in-person support in two states, and a legal dispute may delay Alaska's Senate result.

Counterview. National poll leads do not translate directly into seats, and Trump said he cancelled the rallies because he wanted to campaign by phone, not because of his health.

Storyline · Latin America

Politics & Governance

Latin America ▲ escalating

What happened. Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost to Lula by 4.4 million votes in a national run-off, called himself leader of Brazil in a letter from Miami and alleged fraud without evidence. In Caracas, María Corina Machado returned from exile and said the United States has proposed a presidential election in 2027. Delcy Rodríguez said elections will be held but set no date. [43] [44] Established

Context. Lula won Brazil's Oct. 25 run-off for a fourth term, and the United States seized Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro in January and then backed his vice-president Delcy Rodríguez as interim leader. Both transitions now run through Washington.

Who is Flávio Bolsonaro Far-right Brazilian senator, defeated in the Oct. 25 run-off.

Who is Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva Left-wing president of Brazil, re-elected for a fourth term.

Who is María Corina Machado Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner who has said she would run for president again.

Who is Delcy Rodríguez Venezuela's interim president and former vice-president under Nicolás Maduro, backed by the Trump administration.

Who is Donald Trump US president, whose administration seized Maduro and backed Rodríguez as interim leader.

What changed. Yesterday's entries recorded Bolsonaro's exit via Argentina and Ecuador. Machado's return to Venezuela is new in the arc and is the first date for elections named by a major actor.

Why now. Bolsonaro's claim keeps his base mobilised from abroad while Brazilian courts pursue him over his passports. Machado needs a vote to convert her support into office, while Rodríguez holds power and an oil deal with favourable terms for the United States.

Who gains, who loses. Lula's government faces an opposition leader beyond its courts' reach. Venezuela's opposition gains a public US-backed timetable, while Rodríguez keeps control of the process for now.

Counterview. Bolsonaro's supporters point to the extended polling hours, but both campaigns requested the extension, and BBC Verify found no basis for the fraud claim.

Link. Energy and commodities: Rodríguez's interim government signed an oil deal granting favourable terms to the United States.

Connects to. Elections and political shifts worldwide, Latin America. Driver: US influence over South American transitions

Geopolitics & Security

Africa and the Sahel ▲ escalating

What happened. The US Treasury sanctioned Rwanda's defence ministry, saying it directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 in eastern DR Congo. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Rwanda must halt its support for M23 and withdraw its troops. Washington says minerals from rebel-held areas, including the Rubaya coltan zone, enter Rwanda's supply chains. [56] Reported Single source

SBScott BessentUS Treasury secretaryNo licensed portrait found; initials shown.MM23Rebel group in eastern DR Congo that seized Goma and Bukavu in 2025No licensed portrait found; initials shown.
Read the full analysis

Context. M23 rebels seized Goma and Bukavu in early 2025, and Rwanda and the DR Congo signed the US-brokered Washington Accords in December 2025. Fighting has continued since.

Who is Scott Bessent US Treasury secretary, who announced the sanctions.

Who is M23 Rebel group in eastern DR Congo that seized Goma and Bukavu in 2025.

Minerals link. USGS 2026 data put DR Congo's share of world tantalum mine output at 52.3% and Rwanda's at 16.1%.

What changed. Sanctioning a government ministry is a step beyond the pressure recorded earlier in the arc and the first US sanctions in the record aimed at enforcing the Washington Accords.

Why now. Washington is using financial pressure to hold Rwanda to an accord it brokered, and the accord also aimed to expand regional trade and investment.

Who gains, who loses. Rwanda's defence ministry loses access to the US financial system. Minerals buyers face more scrutiny of supplies routed through Rwanda.

Counterview. Rwanda denies backing M23, and its supporters argue it faces security threats from armed groups in eastern Congo.

Link. Critical minerals: M23 holds Rubaya, a major coltan-producing area, and Washington alleges Rwanda exports more minerals than it produces.

Connects to. Critical minerals, Africa and the Sahel. Driver: Control of eastern Congo's mineral areas

Follow the money.

  • Minerals from rebel-held eastern Congo into Rwandan supply chains, as alleged by Washington: Buyers of Rwandan mineral exports → M23 and Rwandan intermediaries, according to the US Treasury. Sources do not give a figure. (2026-10-29) [56]
